Reviewers say Remy AI is most useful when it turns sleep data into clear, practical next steps. People like the supportive tone, routines, graphs, and integrations such as Apple Watch, saying the app helps them notice patterns and make small habit changes that improve sleep. The main complaints are familiar: some advice feels basic or not personalized enough, notifications can be noisy, and parts of the interface or feature discovery still feel cluttered or confusing. Overall, feedback is strongly positive but points to room for deeper insights and smoother usability.

results.title: Fordham Introduces Remy AI – The Fordham Ram
results.content:
Remy’s abilities also extend to conversations about students’ personal problems. When handling personal situations and hardships, Remy offers advice and invites students to discuss their feelings further. In testing, when the user confided in Remy about a breakup, it offered general emotional support and invited the user to continue discussing their feelings, asking, “If you want, you can talk to me about whether you’re feeling sad, angry, or just numb.” Remy’s ability to respond to emotional concerns could spark debate over students turning to AI for support rather than relying on friends, family or counselors.

Nicholas Smyth, a Fordham professor who teaches ethics of technology, said this ease of turning to a chatbot could come at the expense of the human connections students need. [...] For those who already serve in support roles on campus, Remy has raised questions about how AI could affect their relationships with students.  
 Resident Assistant (RA) Nyah Rodriguez, GSB ’29, said she would likely not recommend Remy to her residents.

“As an RA, I likely wouldn’t recommend Remy to my residents as it would not only take away from my job, but do it poorly,” Rodriguez said. “The AI is not very personable.”

For Rodriguez, the concern is less about Remy’s ability to answer questions and more about whether it can provide the personal connection students may seek from an RA.

“Especially when I felt so comfortable communicating with my RAs last year,” Rodriguez said. “My goal is to provide that same level of comfort and open communication for my residents.” [...] John Villavicencio, FCRH ’28, raised similar concerns about the effect of AI on human interaction at Fordham.

“I don’t like Fordham’s use of AI as it gives less incentive for human interaction,” Villavicencio said. “The use of AI leads to other roles, such as counselors and others, to most likely have less of a use. Most likely, this will be the start of those jobs being less important.”

Rainey said the university does not view Remy as a replacement for Fordham’s existing human support systems. She highlighted the updates made to the Remy FAQ page within the last week in response to student concerns, which state that Remy is “not at all” intended to replace human support.
